www.gtu.edu.tr
One executable, two independent processes
Two users can start the same editor executable. Each running instance has its own PID, current 
instruction position and writable data. One editor can wait for keyboard input while the other is saving 
a file.
The kernel may share physical pages containing read-only code. That implementation choice does 
not make the editors’ ordinary writable variables shared: the address-space abstraction preserves 
their separate views.
Prediction: if one editor crashes, must the other terminate? Normally no. Process isolation limits direct 
interference, although both can still depend on the same external file, service or machine.

What belongs to a process?
Code, static data, dynamically allocated objects 
and stacks occupy a process’s virtual address 
space.
The stack supports active calls; the heap 
supports dynamic allocation. These are useful 
conceptual regions.
Registers and the program counter describe 
current execution; they are not extra regions in 
this memory diagram.
The drawing is schematic. Real layouts include 
mappings and libraries, and their addresses and 
growth directions vary.
OSC 10e, Chapter 3, slide 6

www.gtu.edu.tr
Locate data before explaining its lifetime
A local variable normally belongs to an active function invocation; its lifetime ends when execution 
leaves the relevant scope. A dynamically allocated object remains available until released, subject to 
the language’s rules.
A pointer is an address value, not ownership or permission by itself. Keeping a pointer after an 
object’s lifetime ends does not keep the object alive. Likewise, copying a pointer to another process 
does not establish shared memory.
The diagram’s text, data, heap and stack regions are conceptual. Libraries, mapped files and guard 
regions also occupy virtual addresses. Exact locations and growth directions are not universal.

The kernel must remember more than memory
Identity and state: PID, relationships, scheduling 
information.
Saved execution context: instruction position and 
registers.
Resource references: memory mappings and 
open files.
A PCB is a conceptual summary of these 
records.
OSC 10e, Chapter 3, slide 10
Silberschatz, Galvin & Gagne
CSE513   Lecture 1 14

www.gtu.edu.tr
A process record is not a memory snapshot
To resume a task, the kernel needs its saved processor context and references to its resources. A 
program counter tells where to continue; saved registers preserve values that were live when 
execution stopped.
The address space usually remains represented by memory mappings and resident or backing 
storage. A context switch does not copy every byte of that space into the PCB and then copy it back.
The PCB picture summarizes responsibilities. Real kernels split information among related structures, 
and per-thread context must be distinguished from resources shared by the whole process.

Running, ready and waiting
Running means currently executing on a CPU. 
Ready means able to execute but awaiting 
selection.
Waiting means an event is missing; more CPU 
time alone cannot complete the blocked 
operation.
When input arrives, a waiting task normally 
becomes ready. It need not run immediately.
This is a simplified model; real kernels have 
more states and commonly schedule threads or 
tasks.
OSC 10e, Chapter 3, slide 9
Silberschatz, Galvin & Gagne
CSE513   Lecture 1 16

www.gtu.edu.tr
Ready and waiting require different remedies
Ready: a calculation has all its input and could execute immediately if selected. Its current obstacle is 
processor allocation, so scheduling policy affects its delay.
Waiting: a client has requested a reply that has not arrived. It cannot finish the operation merely by 
receiving another CPU time slice. The missing event must occur first.
A responsive system can run ready work while other tasks wait. This improves use of available 
resources, but it does not shorten the external event itself. “Not running” is therefore an incomplete 
diagnosis.
CSE513   Lecture 1 17

www.gtu.edu.tr
Work through a state trace
P is selected and starts calculating: ready → running.
P requests input that is not available: running → waiting.
The input arrives: waiting → ready.
P is selected again: ready → running.
Its time slice expires: running → ready.
CSE513   Lecture 1 18

www.gtu.edu.tr
Worked trace: who can run now?
Assume one CPU. At time 0, A runs and B is ready. A requests unavailable disk data: A becomes 
waiting and B can be selected. This is a possible execution order, not a measured trace.
While B runs, A’s I/O completes. A becomes ready. B may continue until a scheduling decision selects 
A; I/O completion alone does not prove an immediate switch.
If B then blocks for keyboard input, it becomes waiting. A can run because its earlier dependency is 
satisfied. Track two separate facts at every step: eligibility to run and current CPU ownership.
CSE513   Lecture 1 19

www.gtu.edu.tr
Queues represent different kinds of delay
Ready work competes for processor time.
Waiting work is associated with an event or 
resource.
Completing the event moves work toward 
execution.
Scheduling policy decides which ready task runs 
next.
OSC 10e, Chapter 3, slide 15
Silberschatz, Galvin & Gagne
CSE513   Lecture 1 20

www.gtu.edu.tr
CPU work and I/O waits alternate
A program’s execution often contains CPU bursts separated by waits. Parsing buffered data may be 
CPU work; requesting unavailable input may lead to a wait. The same application can change 
behavior across phases.
A CPU-bound workload spends much of its time ready or running. An I/O-bound workload frequently 
waits for external operations. These descriptions are relative to the workload and system, not 
permanent labels attached to an executable.
When one process waits, another ready process can use the CPU. This is the basic motivation for 
multiprogramming. Week 2 develops the scheduling policies and the instructor’s mechanic/car 
analogy.
CSE513   Lecture 1 21

www.gtu.edu.tr
A context switch preserves continuity
Save the outgoing task’s execution context.
Select and restore another runnable task.
Resume that task where it previously stopped.
Switching costs time and can disturb caches and 
translations.
OSC 10e, Chapter 3, slide 16
Silberschatz, Galvin & Gagne
CSE513   Lecture 1 22

www.gtu.edu.tr
What changes when execution moves from P to Q?
Before the switch, the processor contains values belonging to P’s current execution. The kernel 
records the necessary state so P can later continue correctly; it then restores Q’s saved context.
When P and Q use different address spaces, the execution environment must select the appropriate 
mappings. This need not mean copying all memory or flushing every cache; details depend on the 
architecture and kernel.
The direct save/restore work and indirect working-set effects are overhead. A useful scheduling policy 
balances responsiveness and fairness against the cost of switching too frequently.
CSE513   Lecture 1 23

www.gtu.edu.tr
Kernel entry is not a context switch
P calls a service and returns: P may run throughout.
P blocks inside the service: another task may run.
A timer interrupt occurs: the scheduler may keep P or select Q.
Ask two questions: did privilege change; did the task change?
CSE513   Lecture 1 24

www.gtu.edu.tr
Classify the event, then classify the switch
Case A: P requests a service; the result is immediately available; the kernel returns to P. There is 
kernel entry and return, but no task switch is required.
Case B: P requests unavailable input and blocks; Q is selected. Kernel entry is followed by a task 
switch because P is no longer runnable.
Case C: a timer interrupt arrives while P runs. The scheduler can keep P or choose another task. The 
interrupt is evidence of an event, not evidence that Q necessarily ran.
CSE513   Lecture 1 25

A process is waiting for a network reply. Would a free CPU help?
A read completes immediately. Must another process run?
Two programs finish “at the same time.” Does that prove parallelism?
Explain each answer using state, mode or CPU ownership.

www.gtu.edu.tr
Checkpoint answers and the first-half boundary
A free CPU cannot supply a missing network reply. The waiting task needs the event; only after it 
becomes runnable can CPU selection help it continue.
An immediately completed read can return to the same task. Kernel execution on behalf of P must not 
be confused with scheduling a different task.
Similar finish times do not prove parallelism. One core can interleave several activities. After the 
break, we will follow process creation and examine what changes when several threads share one 
address space.

Launching a command: three separate operations
fork: create a child process.
exec: replace the calling process’s program image.
wait: observe a child’s termination and collect its status.
A shell can use optimized mechanisms; this is the conceptual model.

A process tree records parent–child 
relationships, not which process is currently 
running. A parent may be waiting, computing or 
handling other work while its children execute.
The displayed PIDs are examples from the 
textbook. On your own machine, process names 
and ancestry depend on the shell, service 
manager and environment.
A parent can create several children. A child can 
create further descendants. The tree alone does

OSC 10e, Chapter 3, slide 22
Silberschatz, Galvin & Gagne

www.gtu.edu.tr
fork returns into two processes
Parent receives the child PID; child receives zero.
Both continue after fork, following different branches.
Ordinary memory is logically independent after the fork.
Linux commonly delays copying pages until a write requires it.
CSE513   Lecture 1 30

www.gtu.edu.tr
Follow the return values from fork
Consider a successful fork in a single-threaded program. The parent receives a positive result 
containing the child’s PID; the child receives zero. Both resume after the call, but an if statement 
selects different branches.
If fork fails, the original process receives −1 and no child was created. Error handling must happen 
before treating the result as a valid child identifier.
There is no general guarantee that the parent’s next statement runs before the child’s next statement. 
If the order matters, establish it with synchronization instead of assuming a convenient scheduler 
decision.
CSE513   Lecture 1 31

www.gtu.edu.tr
Copy-on-write preserves separate memory views
Immediately after fork, parent and child have logically separate writable address spaces with initially 
matching contents. A kernel can let their mappings refer to the same physical pages until one needs 
to write.
On a write that requires separation, the operating system arranges a private writable copy. The 
implementation saves unnecessary copying when the child soon replaces its image with exec.
The observable rule for an ordinary variable is unchanged: the child’s assignment does not update 
the parent’s variable. Copy-on-write is an optimization of copying semantics, not a shared-memory 
communication channel.
CSE513   Lecture 1 32

www.gtu.edu.tr
exec changes the program, not the PID
The calling process receives a new program image.
Successful exec does not return to the old program.
On failure, exec returns and the caller must handle the error.
A child can become /bin/echo while remaining the same child process.
CSE513   Lecture 1 33

www.gtu.edu.tr
Prepare the child before replacing its image
A shell can arrange a child’s file descriptors before exec. For example, it can connect the child’s 
standard output to a pipe so that the new program writes to another program’s input.
Exec replaces code, data and the execution stack with the new program image. The PID remains the 
same. Some process attributes survive; others are reset or replaced according to the API’s rules.
Open descriptors generally survive unless marked close-on-exec. This is why setup performed before 
exec can affect the new program. It is also why unintended descriptor inheritance can cause bugs.
CSE513   Lecture 1 34

www.gtu.edu.tr
Launch example: predict the successful output
The child executes /bin/echo, which prints “child” and terminates. The parent calls waitpid for that 
child and prints its status only after termination has been collected.
Therefore the successful output is “child”, followed by “parent: child exit status = 0”. Waiting creates 
the required ordering; the example does not depend on the parent or child winning the first CPU time 
slice.
The complete launch.c checks fork failure, retries waitpid after EINTR, and interprets status with 
WIFEXITED/WEXITSTATUS. These checks belong to the program even when a slide shows only its 
central control flow.
CSE513   Lecture 1 36

www.gtu.edu.tr
Launch example: what happens when exec fails?
Replace /bin/echo with a nonexistent pathname in a copy of the source. Exec now returns with an 
error instead of replacing the child’s program. The child prints an error message and exits with status 
127.
The parent still waits successfully for its child; waiting itself did not fail. It observes exit status 127 and 
reports failure. Separate failure to launch the requested program from failure of the wait operation.
The child uses _exit after failed exec. In this single-threaded example that avoids an additional flush 
of inherited stdio buffers. Status 127 is the example’s chosen failure convention, not a success return 
from exec.
CSE513   Lecture 1 37

www.gtu.edu.tr
wait is synchronization and cleanup
The parent can work while its child executes.
waitpid can block until the selected child terminates.
Termination leaves status information for the parent to collect.
A zombie is terminated; it is not still executing the program.
CSE513   Lecture 1 38

www.gtu.edu.tr
Termination, zombies and parent lifetime
A child that has terminated may retain a small kernel record until its status is collected. This is a 
zombie: its program is no longer executing, although an identifier and termination information remain.
A parent can perform useful work before waiting. Background execution does not remove the 
responsibility to arrange child-status collection; it changes when and how completion is handled.
A process whose parent exits is a different situation from a zombie. Unix-like systems arrange 
reparenting and eventual reaping; the exact responsible process depends on the environment. Do not 
infer either condition merely from “not running”.
CSE513   Lecture 1 39

Observe a process in Ubuntu
sleep 20 &
demo_pid=$!
ps -o pid,ppid,stat,comm -p "$demo_pid"
wait "$demo_pid"
A snapshot shows one moment; it is not a complete execution trace.
CSE513   Lecture 1 40

www.gtu.edu.tr
Interpret a ps observation carefully
PID identifies the observed process; PPID identifies its current parent. STAT summarizes state and 
may include additional flags. COMM names the command; it is not a complete explanation of the 
process’s behavior.
On Linux, R includes running or runnable, so a snapshot does not directly reveal the textbook 
distinction between running and ready. A sleeping state also does not by itself identify the precise 
missing event.
Record what was actually observed. Do not substitute an invented PID or assume a screenshot 
captures every transition. If sleep has already terminated before ps runs, an absent process row is a 
timing outcome, not proof that launch failed.

A thread is an execution stream
Each thread has its own instruction position, 
register state and stack for its active calls.
Threads within a process share the address 
space and many process resources, including 
open files.
A pointer can allow one thread to access an 
object another thread uses, including a live stack 
object.
Separate stacks organize execution. They do not 
impose memory-protection boundaries between 
threads.
OSC 10e, Chapter 4, slide 5
Silberschatz, Galvin & Gagne
CSE513   Lecture 1 42

www.gtu.edu.tr
Compare a process boundary with a thread boundary
Two ordinary processes have separate virtual address spaces. Exchanging data normally requires an 
explicit mechanism, such as a pipe or a shared mapping. This separation provides a useful protection 
boundary.
Two threads in one process share its address space. They have separate registers, instruction 
positions and stacks, but can access common objects. This reduces the need to move data across an 
interface.
The tradeoff is fault containment: an erroneous thread can corrupt shared memory used by other 
threads. Choosing threads because communication is convenient also means accepting responsibility 
for synchronization and object lifetime.
CSE513   Lecture 1 43

www.gtu.edu.tr
Concurrency and parallelism
Concurrency: several activities make progress 
over overlapping periods.
One core can interleave their execution.
Parallelism: activities execute simultaneously on 
different cores.
More threads do not automatically mean faster 
execution.
OSC 10e, Chapter 4, slide 9 (multicore figure)
Silberschatz, Galvin & Gagne
CSE513   Lecture 1 44

www.gtu.edu.tr
Interleaving can create apparent simultaneity
One core executes one thread at a time. T1, T2 
and T3 progress over the same interval because 
the CPU alternates among them.
A user may perceive several activities as 
happening together. That observation 
demonstrates overlapping activity, not 
necessarily simultaneous instruction execution.
On multiple cores, some of these threads may 
truly run in parallel. Correct shared-data 
reasoning must allow the relevant interleavings 
in either case; one core does not make every 
multi-step operation indivisible.
 OSC 10e, Chapter 4, slide 9 (single-core figure)
Silberschatz, Galvin & Gagne

www.gtu.edu.tr
More threads can add work without adding speed
If a task must perform one serial stage before its parallel stage, adding workers cannot remove that 
serial dependency. Workers also consume memory and require creation, scheduling and 
coordination.
A shared lock, limited memory bandwidth or slow storage can become the limiting resource. Beyond 
that point, extra runnable threads may mainly add contention and switching.
For this lecture, distinguish a design’s potential for concurrency from a measured speedup claim. A 
fair performance comparison needs a stated workload, environment and measurement method; our 
diagrams are not benchmark results.

www.gtu.edu.tr
Why a server uses threads
One execution stream accepts incoming work.
Workers can service independent requests.
A blocked request need not stop every other 
request.
Shared caches and queues need coordination.
OSC 10e, Chapter 4, slide 6
Silberschatz, Galvin & Gagne

www.gtu.edu.tr
A bounded worker pool makes ownership explicit
A server can accept requests into a queue and have a bounded set of workers process them. The 
queue separates arrival from service and limits the number of active execution streams.
The design still needs rules: who owns each request, who may change the queue, what happens 
when it is full, and how shutdown wakes waiting workers. Sharing a queue does not answer these 
questions automatically.
Threads are one approach. Event-driven designs can also overlap waiting operations. The 
appropriate model depends on the work; the textbook’s “create a thread” picture is a motivation, not a 
requirement for every server.
CSE513   Lecture 1 48

www.gtu.edu.tr
A shared variable needs a protocol
Suppose increment means: read counter, add one, write counter.
A reads 0; B reads 0.
A writes 1; B writes 1.
Two increments should produce 2, but this interleaving produces 1.
This is a conceptual trace, not valid unsynchronized C code.
CSE513   Lecture 1 49

www.gtu.edu.tr
Explain the lost update one step at a time
Initial counter = 0. A reads 0 into its temporary value. Before A writes, B also reads 0 into its own 
temporary value. Both now plan to store 1.
A writes 1; B subsequently writes 1. B’s write replaces the same value rather than adding to A’s 
already completed update. The intended final value 2 has been lost.
The lesson is to protect the complete operation or use a suitable atomic operation. This is a 
conceptual trace. Unsynchronized conflicting accesses in C can be undefined behavior, so do not 
promise this exact result from a racy C experiment.

www.gtu.edu.tr
Safe sharing in a small thread example
Main initializes a worker argument and starts a thread.
The worker computes a result in that shared object.
Main calls pthread_join before reading the result.
The object remains alive until the worker has finished.
See examples/thread_join.c for the complete program.
CSE513   Lecture 1 51

www.gtu.edu.tr
Joining establishes order, not mutual exclusion
In thread_join.c, main initializes input = 7 and creates a worker. The worker writes result = 49. Main 
joins the worker before reading that result, so the read occurs after worker completion.
This arrangement is safe because main does not concurrently modify the input or read the result too 
early. The argument object also stays alive until the join has completed.
Joining one worker does not protect arbitrary simultaneous accesses among other running workers. If 
several threads update an object concurrently, a separate coordination mechanism may be required.
CSE513   Lecture 1 52

Processes communicate explicitly
Shared memory: processes access a shared 
region.
Message passing: data crosses a 
communication interface.
Both need agreement about meaning, order and 
ownership.
Sharing storage alone does not provide 
synchronization.
OSC 10e, Chapter 3, slide 30
Silberschatz, Galvin & Gagne
CSE513   Lecture 1 53

www.gtu.edu.tr
Choose a communication model deliberately
Shared memory provides a common region. Participants must agree on layout, ownership and when 
data is ready. A flag in that region still needs correct synchronization; merely sharing the flag is 
insufficient.
Message passing makes an interface explicit: send a request, receive a reply, or consume a stream 
with a defined format. It still needs error handling, ordering rules and a way to distinguish complete 
messages.
Neither approach eliminates protocol design. Ask what must cross the boundary, which participant 
may modify it, how completion is signaled, and what the receiver should do if the sender stops.

A pipe connects output to input
printf 'alpha\nbeta\n' | wc -l
The producer writes a byte stream.
The consumer reads bytes and counts newline characters.
Expected result: 2. Whitespace formatting may vary.
A pipe does not preserve application message boundaries.

www.gtu.edu.tr
A pipeline is a data-flow agreement
For printf followed by wc -l, the producer supplies bytes containing two newline characters. The 
consumer counts newline characters and prints 2. This result follows from the input, not from a 
particular scheduling order.
The shell arranges the input/output connection. It may execute printf as a builtin, so the command 
text alone is not a reliable count of newly created external processes.
A stream can be read in chunks different from the producer’s writes. Programs that exchange records 
must define framing, for example a delimiter or length field, rather than assuming each read returns 
one complete application message.

www.gtu.edu.tr
Blocking and end-of-file are different
Empty pipe + a writer still exists: a blocking read 
may wait.
No writers remain: after buffered bytes are read, 
read returns EOF.
A full pipe can make a blocking writer wait.
Unused pipe ends must be closed so completion 
can be observed.
OSC 10e, Chapter 3, slide 61
Silberschatz, Galvin & Gagne

www.gtu.edu.tr
Backpressure connects communication to waiting
If a producer generates data faster than a consumer removes it, the finite pipe buffer can fill. A 
blocking writer then waits for space; it is not simply ready for more processor time.
If a consumer is faster, it may drain the buffer and wait for data while writers still exist. This temporary 
emptiness differs from EOF after all writers have closed and buffered bytes are consumed.
These waits couple the participants’ progress. A pipeline can therefore contain processes waiting for 
data or space as well as processes ready for the CPU. Resource cleanup and consumption rate both 
affect completion.

www.gtu.edu.tr
Explain a complete run without skipping boundaries
For each participant, identify its process identity, program image and open communication ends. An 
exec changes the image; it does not create an extra participant. A fork creates a new process with 
inherited state.
At every delay, ask whether the task is ready or waiting and identify the event that can make progress 
possible. At every kernel entry, ask separately whether another task was actually selected.
Finally, account for completion: close unused pipe ends, let readers observe EOF, and collect child 
status. A program that computed the right bytes can still fail to finish if these lifecycle obligations are 
missed.
